notes:
I couldn't do as much research as planned. My tool limit ran out before I reached Catholic and Orthodox sites (newadvent, catholic.com, oca.org), the NET Bible study notes, bibleodyssey, or any site where traditions clearly disagree. I also found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching for this passage. The Enduring Word page I opened stopped partway through verse 21. Points I couldn't find are left out.

**Notes on Mark 15:1–24**

**v. 1:** Guzik says this was the Sanhedrin's official daylight trial. Quoting Lane, he says the early hour fits history: a Roman official's working day started at dawn, so the council had to reach Pilate first thing. He also says the leaders went to Pilate because they had no legal right to carry out executions themselves. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-15/ The Bible Hub study note says Rome alone could approve crucifixion. It adds that handing Jesus to Gentiles fulfilled His own prediction in Mark 10:33. https://biblehub.com/mark/15-2.htm

**v. 2:** Guzik says the leaders called Jesus "King of the Jews" because Pilate would take a political threat to Caesar seriously, but not a religious claim. He reads Jesus' answer as a qualified "yes." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-15/ Bible Hub's note agrees: Jesus affirmed the title without accepting the false political meaning His accusers intended. https://biblehub.com/mark/15-2.htm Its chapter summary calls the Greek phrase *su legeis* a form of affirmation. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/mark/15.htm

**v. 3:** Guzik points to Luke 23:2 for what the charges were: stirring up riots, telling people not to pay taxes, and claiming to be a king against Rome. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-15/

**vv. 4–5:** Guzik, quoting Lane, says silence like this was very unusual in a Roman court. It showed a dignity that puzzled Pilate. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-15/ Bible Hub's summary says the silence fulfilled Isaiah 53:7. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/mark/15.htm

**v. 6:** Peake's Commentary, an older critical work, notes that the custom of releasing a prisoner is not otherwise attested. It may have been a practice adopted by Pilate. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/mark-15.html Guzik says Pilate was caught between doing right and doing what was politically safe. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-15/

**v. 7:** Guzik says the word "insurrectionists" basically amounts to "terrorists." Barabbas was a real political enemy of Rome, not a falsely accused political enemy, as Jesus was. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-15/

There are three readings of the name "Barabbas":
- Guzik and Bible Hub say it means "son of the father," an ironic contrast with Jesus, the true Son. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-15/ https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/mark/15.htm
- Peake reads it as probably "son of the teacher," a fairly common name. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/mark-15.html
- Coffman calls it a patronymic and paraphrases it as "Papa's Boy." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/mark-15.html

**v. 8:** Who made up the crowd is disputed:
- Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) suggests the crowd may have come to win Barabbas's release, perhaps seeing him as a national hero, rather than to see Jesus tried. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/csc/mark-15.html
- Coffman (Restoration Movement) rejects this. He says friends of Barabbas would have had no reason to shout "Crucify him!" https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/mark-15.html
- Guzik says the crowd was mostly Jerusalem locals, because most pilgrims were staying out in the country. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-15/

**vv. 9–10:** Guzik says Pilate saw through the leaders' envy and hoped the Passover custom would let him free Jesus without paying a price. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-15/ Coffman says Pilate, not the crowd, brought up the idea of releasing a prisoner. He counts this as one of Pilate's "seven efforts" to free Jesus. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/mark-15.html

**v. 11:** Guzik thinks the crowd sided with their own Sanhedrin against Rome's governor. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-15/ Bible Hub's application is to be careful about which voices we listen to. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/mark/15.htm

**vv. 12–14:** Guzik thinks Pilate hoped a beating would satisfy the crowd, and was shocked when they demanded crucifixion. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-15/ Bible Hub points out that both Pilate here and the centurion in v. 39 show that Jesus was innocent. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/mark/15.htm

**v. 15:** Guzik's substitution reading: if anyone was able to say, "Jesus died for me," it was Barabbas. He knew what it was to have Jesus die on his behalf, the innocent in the place of the guilty. He also describes the flogging in medical detail, citing a 1986 article in the *Journal of the American Medical Association*, and notes that Roman law required the method of death to be stated. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-15/ Trapp (Puritan) thinks Pilate had Jesus flogged hoping to make the people pity Him, but says this was ill done of Pilate nevertheless. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/mark-15.html

**vv. 16–18:** Guzik says the robe and thorn crown mocked the purple robe and leafy wreath kings wore. The robe was probably a faded scarlet soldier's cloak. "Hail, King of the Jews" twisted the greeting "Hail, Caesar." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-15/

**v. 19:** Guzik, drawing on Matthew 27:29, says the staff was first handed to Jesus as a mock scepter, then used to beat Him. The Greek tense means they kept on spitting. Kneeling mocked the respect normally shown a king. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-15/

**v. 20:** Guzik says the march to execution advertised Rome's power to frighten people. He links it to Jesus' call to "take up your cross and follow Me" (Mark 8:34). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-15/

**v. 21:** Nearly every commentator thinks Mark names Simon's sons because his readers knew them. Many link this Rufus with the Rufus of Romans 16:13:
- Guzik suggests Simon later learned what it truly means to carry the cross. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-15/
- Ellicott takes this further. He thinks Simon's wife may have been the "mother" Paul greets in Romans 16:13, and links the family to the "men of Cyrene" in Acts 11:20. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/15-21.htm
- MacLaren suggests Simon may be "Simeon called Niger" in Acts 13:1. He traces Simon moving from forced labour to willing service. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/expositions-of-holy-scripture/mark/simon-the-cyrenian.cfm
- Gill is more cautious: he says it is not certain these are the same men. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/15-21.htm

Applications: Trapp says God rewards even service done unwillingly. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/mark-15.html Matthew Henry says we should not be surprised when crosses come on us suddenly. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/15-21.html

Simon's ethnicity is disputed. Constable thinks he was probably... racially a Semite rather than a Negro. The Light of Israel commentary says he was obviously a person of color. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/15-21.html

**v. 22:** Explanations of the name "Place of the Skull":
- Gill: the story that Adam's skull was found there is an ancient tradition "without foundation." He thinks the name came from it being a place of execution. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nlv/matthew/27-33.html
- Barnes: no one knows for certain why it got the name. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/27-33.html
- Lutheran (1517.org): the early church understood Golgotha as Adam's grave, with the second Adam's cross set over the first Adam's grave. Most crucifixion icons show Adam's skull at the foot of the cross. https://www.1517.org/articles/golgotha-the-place-of-adams-skull
- Got Questions disagrees. It says Jesus was most likely *not* crucified over Adam's tomb, and notes that Origen, Chrysostom and Jerome mentioned the story without accepting it. It adds that Greek Orthodox icons almost always show the skull. https://www.gotquestions.org/tomb-of-Adam.html
- The NET Bible dictionary (ISBE entry) says the idea that the hill is skull-shaped is quite modern, and the Gospels give no evidence it was on a hill. https://classic.net.bible.org/dictionary.php?word=golgotha

**v. 23:** Why was the wine offered, and why did Jesus refuse it?
- Cambridge Bible: it was a merciful Jewish custom, based on Proverbs 31:6, to dull the senses of the condemned. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/15-23.htm
- Peake: the Jewish practice used frankincense, not myrrh, and myrrh doesn't make you drowsy. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/mark-15.html
- Guzik: Jesus needed a clear mind to bear the Father's wrath as our substitute. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-15/
- Coffman, following Cranfield: the refusal kept Jesus' vow in Mark 14:25 not to drink wine again until the kingdom. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/15-23.html
- Bible Hub: Jesus chose to face the cross fully conscious, and the refusal also fits the Mark 14:25 vow. https://biblehub.com/study/mark/15-23.htm

**v. 24:** Bible Hub says this fulfils Psalm 22:18 (the garments) and Psalm 22:16 (pierced hands and feet). Roman executioners were allowed to keep a victim's clothes. https://biblehub.com/mark/15-24.htm Gill explains that the clothes were split four ways among the soldiers, and they cast lots for the seamless coat. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nas/mark/15-24.html Henry says the soldiers were enjoying themselves amid His misery. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/15-22.html The Pulpit Commentary argues that Psalm 22's details never fit David himself. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/psalms-22.html

**Where the sources disagree:** The only real disagreements I found were:
- Adam's skull at Golgotha (Lutheran 1517.org for; Gill and Got Questions against)
- the reason for refusing the wine (clear mind for the atonement vs. keeping the Mark 14:25 vow)
- who the crowd was (Chuck Smith vs. Coffman)
- Simon's ethnicity (Constable vs. Light of Israel)

None of these is a clear split between Baptist, Methodist, Pentecostal, Reformed or Lutheran teaching.
